findings.claim: Every lesson's 8-mark question is typed '8 marks — Discuss*' and footnoted '*Quality of written communication assessed.'
findings.truth: R180 awards no marks for quality of written communication or SPaG. The exam is 1h15 and 70 marks, Section A 25 and Section B 45, and the Performance Objectives are PO1 recall, PO2 apply and PO3 analyse and evaluate. Footnote and asterisk removed in all ten lessons.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2 assessment guidance and 4.1.5 Performance Objectives; no SPaG or written-communication wording anywhere in the spec

findings.claim: Key fact: 'Intrinsic factors fall into four areas: individual variables ... physical preparation (warm-up, nutrition, hydration), psychological factors ... mental strategies'. The description repeats 'physical preparation'.
findings.truth: The spec's four intrinsic sub-topics are individual variables (1.2.1), psychological factors (1.2.2), reasons for aggression (1.2.3) and mental strategies (1.2.4). Nutrition/hydration and sleep sit inside individual variables. 'Physical preparation' is not a spec category, and the lesson body itself teaches reasons for aggression.

findings.claim: Description: 'individual variables (age, flexibility, fitness), physical preparation, and psychological factors'.
findings.truth: Same scope error as F2, and flexibility is part of fitness levels rather than a listed variable. Description rewritten to the spec's grouping and shortened to 89 characters.

findings.claim: 'Owen Farrell has a well-known routine before every free kick where he mentally rehearses the kicking action.'
findings.truth: A free kick in rugby union cannot be kicked at goal. Farrell's routine precedes a kick at goal (penalty or conversion).
findings.evidence: Laws of rugby union: a free kick may not be taken as a kick at goal

findings.claim: Static stretching is taught as one of the two stretch types 'used in warm ups'; the worked rugby warm up includes 'brief static holds (15–20 seconds)'; the collapsible says static stretching 'is best performed after the pulse raiser'; the description lists warm-up stretching as 'static, dynamic, PNF'.
findings.truth: The spec's warm-up components (2.1.1) are pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching and a skill rehearsal phase. Maintenance stretches, static stretches and PNF are cool-down components (2.3.2). A student naming static stretching as a warm-up component risks no credit. NHS guidance likewise places static stretching after exercise.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.1 and 2.3.2; NHS 'How to stretch after exercising'

findings.claim: Mark scheme for 'Identify one component of a warm up' credits '• Stretching (1)'.
findings.truth: The spec names dynamic stretching as the warm-up component. Changed to 'Dynamic stretching (1)'.

findings.claim: 'Lactic acid ... if not removed, it builds up in the muscles and contributes to DOMS'; 'Without a cool down to help remove lactic acid, the severity of DOMS increases significantly'; the 3-mark answer key credits 'It is caused by a build-up of lactic acid/waste products in the muscles'.
findings.truth: DOMS is caused by microscopic damage to muscle fibres from eccentric work and the inflammation that follows. Lactate returns to resting levels within about an hour, far too soon to explain soreness peaking at 24–72 hours. The lesson's own glossary already defines DOMS as 'caused by microscopic damage to muscle fibres', so the content contradicted itself. The spec lists lactic-acid removal and reduced DOMS risk as two separate cool-down benefits, never as cause and effect.
findings.evidence: spec 2.4.1; Wikipedia 'Delayed onset muscle soreness' (lactic acid theory rejected; lactate cleared within one hour)

findings.claim: 'An effective cool down has three main components' — pulse lowering, static stretching and deep breathing/relaxation; the exam tip and the 1-mark answer key both credit deep breathing as a component.
findings.truth: The spec gives two cool-down components: pulse lowering (2.3.1) and stretching (2.3.2: maintenance, static and PNF). Deep breathing is not spec content and would not be credited. Maintenance and PNF stretches were missing entirely. Reframed as two components plus an optional relaxation phase, with the missing stretch types added.

findings.claim: 'Hard tissue injuries — damage to bones (e.g. fractures, dislocations, concussion)', repeated in the conclusion.
findings.truth: Concussion is a brain injury, not damage to bone. The spec treats head injuries (3.1.8) as a group of their own, separate from the soft-tissue and hard-tissue split at 3.1.2.

findings.claim: SALTAPS is taught with the final S as 'Standing: can the player stand up and bear weight?'. The knowledge check marks 'See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active, Passive, Standing' as the correct expansion, and the 4-mark answer key repeats it.
findings.truth: The spec defines SALTAPS as See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active, Passive, Strength. The last stage tests whether the limb can work against resistance. A student who wrote the spec answer would have been marked wrong by the knowledge check.

findings.claim: DRABC occupies two of the five cards: one card with DRABC as the answer, one with 'What is meant by DRABC?' as the question.
findings.truth: Card 4 changed to the recovery position, which is taught in the same lesson and had no card.

findings.claim: The glossary lists DRABC twice, with two different definitions.
findings.truth: The duplicate comes from two <dfn> tags for the same term in the content. Harmless but untidy; removing a glossary row is outside the edit shapes, so left for the next rebuild.

findings.claim: 'If the ambulance takes more than 15 minutes, repeat the cycle of 10 puffs.'
findings.truth: NHS guidance says that if the ambulance has not arrived after 10 minutes and symptoms are not improving, repeat the reliever inhaler up to the same maximum dose. The rest of the asthma sequence in the lesson (1 puff every 30–60 seconds, maximum 10 puffs, sit upright, call 999) matches the NHS exactly.

findings.claim: The glossary lists epilepsy twice ('epilepsy' and 'Epilepsy') with different definitions.
findings.truth: Same cause as F13: two <dfn> tags for one term. Left for the next rebuild.

findings.claim: 'Christian Eriksen ... collapsed on the pitch during Denmark's Euro 2021 match against Finland.'
findings.truth: The tournament kept the name UEFA Euro 2020 although it was postponed and played in 2021. Eriksen collapsed on 12 June 2021 in Denmark's Euro 2020 opener against Finland.

findings.claim: 'This is why sports venues are now required to have accessible AEDs.'
findings.truth: No UK law requires a sports venue to hold a defibrillator. Some governing bodies and funding schemes insist on one, but the duty is not general. Softened to describe the trend rather than a legal duty.
findings.evidence: no statutory requirement exists; the Public Access Defibrillator bill did not pass

findings.claim: Flashcard 4 is a mangled auto-generated cloze: answer 'Christian', question 'One of the most high-profile examples in sport is _____ Eriksen , who collapsed on the pitch during Denmark's Euro 2021 match against Finland'. It has a stray space before the comma, no closing stop, a one-word name as the answer, and it repeats the Euro 2021 error.
findings.truth: Replaced with a spec-relevant card from the same lesson: 'What is meant by hypothermia?' answered by the lesson's own definition. All five answers in the deck stay unique.

findings.claim: Eight data-revision-tip prompts are broken or ungrammatical, e.g. L6 'Write out the formula or equation from memory' on a box with no formula, L10 'Recall the specific examples given for do NOT apply direct heat (such as.', L10 'Describe the process for dehydration directly increases the step by step.', L8 'Describe the process for the injury appears serious at any step by step.'
findings.truth: These are generator artefacts that students read on the page. Each rewritten as a plain question about the box it sits on (lessons 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 ×2).

findings.claim: Hypoglycaemia: 'Check their blood sugar after 15–20 minutes.'
findings.truth: Diabetes UK's rule of 15 is 15g of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes, then re-test. The lesson's window is slightly wide but not wrong, and the spec sets no timing.

findings.claim: 'A thorough warm up should last at least 15–20 minutes', repeated in the conclusion and tested by a knowledge check that marks '5–10 minutes' wrong.
findings.truth: The spec sets no warm-up duration, and NHS guidance says a general warm up should take at least 6 minutes. 15–20 minutes is normal for competitive sport, so the claim is defensible, but it is presented as examinable fact when it is not. Worth softening at the next rebuild rather than editing the knowledge check now.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 sets no duration; NHS 'How to warm up before exercising'

findings.claim: 'Medicals are typically carried out around one month before the intended activity begins' and screening 'usually carried out during the off-season'.
findings.truth: Neither timing appears in the spec (4.1.2 lists only medicals, screening and NGB policies) and neither is traceable to a primary source. Common textbook shorthand; no evidence found either way, so not corrected.

findings.claim: Thirty of the fifty cards put the definition in the question and the bare term in the answer, so the definition often contains the answer's own root word ('Contact sports' answered from a question that says 'physical contact ... sport').
findings.truth: This is the build-wide card format rather than a fault in this unit, and it does not mark anything wrong. Flagged for the deck standard, not edited here.
findings.evidence: deck review across all ten lessons

summary: Ten lessons checked against the R180 teaching content and assessment guidance. Four HIGH errors: static stretching taught as a warm-up component (spec puts it in the cool down), DOMS blamed on lactic acid in the content and in a mark scheme, SALTAPS taught and answer-keyed as ending in Standing rather than Strength, and a mangled Eriksen cloze flashcard. All ten lessons footnoted the 8-mark question with a quality-of-written-communication claim the spec does not make. Medical and first-aid content is otherwise sound: PRICE, DRABC, the recovery position, CPR ratios, asthma puff counts, the 5-minute seizure rule, 35 and 38 degree thresholds and the CRY 14-35 age band all check out. No lesson names the exam board or calls the course a GCSE. 63 edits.
